A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same VER research work. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete appendices are readable and support reliable comparison across relocations and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original distillation experiments, simulated and real-robot task results, routing ablations, and feature analyses, including appendix results.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds a VLA comparison, training-dynamics analyses, and annealing and architecture ablations.

M1.justification: The written CTA schedule changes from L to L+1 inside the decay expression (v1 Eq. 6 versus v2 Eq. 7). Mutual-information probabilities are also described using router scores rather than selection counts (v1 Appendix C.2 versus v2 D.2). These are localized revisions to the specified procedure; the PDFs do not establish whether implementation changes accompanied them.

E1.justification: Both versions use ImageNet-1K, Franka Kitchen, Meta-World, Adroit, LIBERO and its color-shift evaluation, simulated pick-and-place, and real-world pouring. The new comparisons and ablations reuse existing tasks. The 25% ImageNet subset changes experimental settings, not coverage.

E2.justification: v2 adds fine-tuned GR00T N1.5 to the existing three pick-and-place comparisons alongside Theia and VER (Table 10). The other comparator sets are retained.

E3.justification: Existing benchmark protocols remain unchanged. Added experiments introduce 200-epoch CTA-duration sweeps, architectural comparisons using 25% of ImageNet-1K and MLP widths scaled by 1/K, and batch-size-one latency measurements. The new GR00T comparison specifies 20,000 fine-tuning steps with batch size 16.

E4.justification: v2 substantially extends analysis of the central design choices: activation trajectories test when router collapse occurs (Figures 10–11), Appendix B.3 tests annealing duration, and Appendix F tests expert configurations, component latency, and backbone/expert depth. These supplement the retained routing, feature, Top-K, and expert-mixture analyses.

E5.justification: New ablations specify three seeds for annealing duration and five seeds for expert configurations, with uncertainty displays. The original ten-seed mean-and-standard-deviation reporting and regression analysis remain unchanged; no increase in repetitions of existing experiments is established.

E6.justification: Original numerical tables and figure results are retained, including the 74.7% average in Table 1. New results include GR00T N1.5 scores of 0.75, 0.73, and 0.70 (Table 10), annealing results, and architecture/latency measurements. Table 12 newly shows lower distillation loss but lower task success when increasing expert-layer depth. These are added findings under their stated settings, not revised performance on retained experiments.

T1.justification: v2 adds Proposition 1 and Appendix B.1's detailed derivation of router-logit gradients, distinguishing active experts' expert-specific signals from inactive experts' indirect updates. It also adds mutual-information entropy-decomposition reasoning and completes the expert summation in Eq. 3. v1 has no corresponding gradient proposition or derivation.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and conclusion retain the same main contributions and claims: foundation-model distillation into an expert library, lightweight task-adaptive routing, PER with CTA, extensibility, and strong performance across robotic tasks. Added analyses and comparisons support these retained claims.

C2.justification: v2 develops a substantially fuller mechanism explanation connecting collapse to inactive-expert gradients and differing router/policy convergence rates. It explains mutual information through balancing and teacher specialization, and adds interpretations of annealing-duration trade-offs and why excessive expert capacity or depth can hinder downstream transfer despite improved distillation.

D1.justification: v2 documents technical settings for the added experiments, including GR00T fine-tuning, annealing durations, architectural width scaling, reduced pretraining data, and latency batch size. Existing router architecture details, pretraining hardware and schedule, and code/checkpoint release statements remain substantially unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds references to RoboScript, SkillDiffuser, and GR00T, and extends empirical positioning to a fine-tuned VLA model. The principal positioning relative to foundation-model distillation, MoE routing, and visuomotor learning remains unchanged.

P1.justification: Most prose and the main section sequence are retained. Targeted rewrites expand Sections 3.3–3.4 and the architecture/efficiency discussion, while new Appendices B and F shift existing appendix labels. There are also wording edits and a conference-publication header update.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the visual analysis with training-time activation heatmaps, an annealing learning-curve plot, and tables for annealing, VLA comparison, configuration latency, and depth. Original figure images are retained; former appendix Figures 10–15 become Figures 13–18, with additional relocation and page reflow.

improvement.justification: v1 already supported the main performance and CTA findings. v2 strengthens their explanation and the justification of architectural choices through gradient analysis, training trajectories, controlled ablations, and the GR00T comparison. These are useful gains, tempered by a new inconsistency: Eq. 7 gives K(0)=L+1 although the text specifies initialization with L experts. Overall, the added support improves the paper, but the revised procedure still needs clarification.
